activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial, which an oven thermometer placed inside can reveal.
story:
Grandma's kitchen smelled like burnt paper again. Alice stared at the tray of black-topped muffins and thought about last summer, when the same thing had happened with the blueberry batch. She had followed the recipe exactly that time too, measuring the flour level with a knife like Grandma taught her, and the tops still came out scorched while the middles stayed gooey. She had blamed herself then and quit halfway through learning to bake, which she sometimes regretted and sometimes didn't.

"Third time," said Neveah, who had come over to help. "Even Amy's batch burned, and Amy never burns anything."

Alice wiped her hands on her aprapron and thought. The recipe was right. The measurements were right. So something they couldn't see had to be wrong. "It's like guessing what an animal eats without seeing it eat," she said slowly. "You have to look for clues. A rabbit has flat teeth for plants, so you know it's a herbivore. The oven has to be leaving us a clue too."

"What kind of clue does an oven leave?"

Alice opened the cabinet above the fridge, where Grandma kept odd gadgets, and found a shelf so bare it looked almost desolate except for one item: a round metal thermometer with a hook. She hung it inside the oven, set the dial to the recipe's temperature, and waited while the batter sat on the counter in its paper cups.

When the little needle stopped moving, Alice fetched Grandpa's magnifying glass to read the tiny numbers. The dial said one thing. The thermometer said the oven was really twenty-five degrees hotter. "That's it," she said. "Many home ovens run hotter or cooler than the temperature on the dial. This one runs hot. That's why everything burns even when we follow the recipe exactly."

She turned the dial down, waited, and slid in the new tray. Twenty minutes later the muffins came out golden, and Neveah split one open so steam curled into the air.

"Still not sorry you quit last summer?" Neveah asked.

Alice took a bite and pushed the rest of the tray toward her. "Try one and ask me again."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
story:
Brielle arrived at class with her right arm in a bright green cast and a question already forming in her head. Her grandfather had broken his wrist last spring, and she remembered sitting on his porch while he scratched a pencil inside his cast and complained. His had stayed on for weeks after hers came off, and they had broken the same bone, the radius, in nearly the same spot. Why, she wondered, did his break take so much longer?

"Nice cast," said Duke, sliding into the seat beside her. "My grandpa broke his arm last winter. He was in that thing forever. Yours will probably be forever too."

"It won't," Eva said. "Brielle's a kid. Kids heal faster."

"How do you know?" Duke challenged her. "Maybe grown-ups just break bones worse because they're heavier."

Brielle had been thinking about exactly that. She wrote GROWN-UPS? on her notebook with her left hand, which came out wobbly. There was a hidden rule somewhere, and she wanted to find it. She decided on a simple test. She would ask everyone she knew who had ever worn a cast and write down who they were, how they broke the bone, and how long the cast stayed on.

At lunch she collected her data. Her cousin, eleven years old, had a broken forearm in a cast for about four weeks. The crossing guard, who was older than her mother, wore one for her ankle for more than two months. Ms. Marino stopped by their table and added her own entry: she had broken her wrist as an adult and spent a long stretch in a cast, longer than any kid on Brielle's list. By afternoon Brielle had eleven names in her notebook.

"Look," she said, turning the notebook toward Duke. Every kid on the list, even with the same kind of break as an adult, had the cast come off sooner. "Young bones heal faster than adult bones. So kids spend less time in a cast than adults with the same break." She remembered her grandfather then, leaning back in his chair, holding out his wrist to compare with hers, laughing that she would be swimming again while he was still stuck. It had seemed random that afternoon. Now it seemed like a rule.

"Okay," Duke said slowly. "I guess that's pretty objective. The numbers all point the same way." He frowned at the notebook, then brightened. "So my grandpa's long cast wasn't because he was clumsy. It was just because he's old."

"It doesn't signify that he's clumsy at all," Eva said. "It just means his bones take longer."

Ms. Marino leaned over the notebook and tapped one line with her finger. "You know," she said, "collecting evidence like this is real science. It takes patience and honesty, which is worth more than income to a researcher."

Brielle smiled and added a twelfth line, a prediction: MY CAST, four weeks, maybe five. Then she held up the green plaster for Duke to sign.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Anxiety is a normal feeling of worry or fear, but it may be an anxiety disorder when it is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life.
story:
Jack was supposed to be buttering toast, but he kept glancing at the phone on the counter. Leah had texted him four times before eight in the morning, all about the science test they had on Friday, and it was only Tuesday. Her last message read, "What if I throw up in class? I keep thinking about it." Jack typed "you'll be fine" and deleted it, because last week she hadn't been fine. She'd chewed her sleeve during the math quiz until it was soaked, and she hadn't eaten her lunch at all.

He pulled the pamphlet his mother had brought home from the clinic out of the junk drawer, the one with the cartoon heart on the front. His mother was still upstairs, so he read it aloud to himself while the toast went cold. "Anxiety is a normal feeling of worry or fear," he read, "but it may be an anxiety disorder when it is intense, lasts a long time, and gets in the way of daily life." He set the pamphlet next to the phone and counted on his fingers, one for each part. Intense: throwing-up fear over a test three days away. Lasts a long time: she'd been like this since September. Gets in the way: the sleeve, the skipped lunch. Three out of three. It was like checking a recipe, he thought. You couldn't see what was wrong inside a person, but you could test it against the steps.

When his mother came down tying her robe, Jack slid the pamphlet toward her. "Can Leah's mom see this? I think it might be more than regular nerves." He didn't want to be reckless and just tell Leah to relax, because that had made things worse last time. "Will you elaborate on that a little?" his mother asked, so he explained the three checks, and she nodded slowly and said she'd call Leah's mother before school.

At the bus stop, Jack sat next to Leah, who was flipping through her flashcards with trembling hands. He didn't mention tests or pamphlets. Instead he unwrapped the extra toast he'd made and set half on her knee, still warm. "My grandma's recipe," he said. "It's kind of our heritage, she makes it every time somebody in the family has a hard week." Leah looked at the toast, then at him, and took a bite.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
On Saturday morning Matteo counted his money twice, because eleven dollars had a way of feeling like more or less depending on the day. He was saving for a jar of Mr. Romano's honey, the dark kind that his grandmother used to preserve tomatoes in the old country way. At the farmers' market he found Mr. Romano's stall, but there was a line six people deep, and a hand-lettered sign that made his stomach drop: HONEY, $14.

"Fourteen?" Matteo said. "Last month it was nine."

Mr. Romano shrugged. "Bad year for the bees. I have twelve jars and, look around, more than twelve people." Sure enough, by the time Matteo reached the front, three jars were left, and a woman bought two of them at once. Matteo walked away empty-handed and found his friend Louise at the tomato stand, where a pyramid of tomatoes sat so tall it cast shade.

"Look at this," Louise said. "The tomato guy is yelling three dollars a basket, and nobody's even stopping. He's got more tomatoes than the whole market could eat." As they watched, the man crossed out his sign and wrote TWO DOLLARS. A small crowd formed. By the time the baskets were nearly gone, he crossed it out again and wrote THREE, and the last few sold anyway.

Matteo pulled out the notebook he carried for exactly this kind of thing. "So when there's lots, the price falls until people buy it all. When there's little, the price climbs until only a few people still want it."

"Mr. Romano said a word for that yesterday," Louise said. "The price where buyers want exactly as much as sellers have, he called it the market-clearing price."

Matteo wrote it down. Back at the honey stall, the last jar sat unsold at fourteen dollars, and Mr. Romano was frowning at it. Matteo waited, then held up his eleven dollars. "I have this much. And the market closes in twenty minutes, and I'm the only one standing here."

Mr. Romano rubbed his chin, thinking of revenue lost on an unsold jar. "Eleven," he said at last, "and you do me a favor." From under the table he pulled a mason jar of cloudy, cream-colored stuff. "This is mandatory for every kid who buys from me. It's whipped honey. Tell your friends where it came from."

That night Matteo wrote a note and slid it under Louise's door: "Dear Louise. Got the honey for eleven. Also, the tomato man ended with zero tomatoes and the honey man ended with zero honey, and I think that means something. Meet me at the market next Saturday. Bring your allowance. Bring the notebook. Bring snacks, because the snack stand had a line out to the parking lot, and you know what that means. Your friend, Matteo."

Louise read the note twice, then went to find her piggy bank.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In the United States, a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for 12 months.
story:
The morning after the movers left, Victor sat on the floor of the empty new house and wrote his old address on thirty envelopes, one for every kid in his class back in Maplewood. Lyric had promised to write back weekly, though Victor suspected she would persevere for about two weeks before switching to texting.

"Give the mail a chance," his dad said, dragging a box toward the kitchen. "I filed the permanent change of address with the Postal Service at the counter yesterday."

"What does that even do?" Victor asked.

"First-Class Mail gets forwarded to the new address for twelve months," his dad said, and then he dropped the box on his foot and said a word Victor was not allowed to repeat.

So Victor had one year, exactly. He tested the idea the first week by mailing himself a postcard at the old address, and eight days later it arrived at the new house with a yellow sticker on it, routed like a homing pigeon. He grinned and showed Lyric's first letter to his new neighbor Yosef over the fence. Yosef, who wanted nothing more than a teammate for the basketball net bolted to his garage, studied the envelope like it was a scout report.

"Twelve months," Yosef said. "So if somebody mailed you a scholarship application in month eleven, it would still find you. That's actually wild."

"It's ironic, actually," Victor said. "I spent two months dreading this move, and the mail is the only thing that followed me."

They played one-on-one until the streetlights buzzed on, and Yosef won four games to three by using a sneaky left-hand layup he claimed he'd been hiding since March. Victor went inside sweaty and cheerful and found two more letters on the hall table. He held them up like trophies.

"Dad," he called toward the kitchen, "eleven months and three weeks left. I'm keeping count."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way.
story:
The bus stopped in front of the fire station with an abrupt hiss of brakes, and Connor was the first one down the steps. He had been wondering all week what a real station would look like inside, and it was better than he'd pictured: tall doors, poles, and a big old engine polished until it glowed.

Mr. Chea counted heads while a firefighter led them past the lockers. Near the old engine, a painting of a spotted dog hung in a gold frame. Caleigh squinted at it. "Why would they put a dog picture next to a truck?" she asked. "It's not even a fire dog. It's just... spotty."

Connor studied the painting instead of guessing right away. The engine in the picture looked older than the one beside it, with wooden wheels and a long pole where the ladder went. Were the horses pulling it? He counted them: four horses, and the spotted dog running out in front. He turned the question over. The dog wasn't riding, and it wasn't chasing the engine. It was ahead of the horses, on the road. Why would a dog run ahead?

"There's a logbook on that shelf," he said, pointing to a ledger beside the frame. "From back then." He asked the firefighter if he could look, and she said sure. Connor assessed the faded pages, flipping past alarms and repairs until he found a note from an old captain: "The dog cleared the street ahead better than any whistle. The horses trust him." Yasmin leaned over his shoulder. "Trust him? Horses don't even like dogs usually."

"That's it, though," Connor said slowly, testing the idea as he said it. "These dogs got along with horses. That's the whole reason firehouses kept them. The horses pulled the engines, and the dog ran ahead, clearing the way." He tapped the painting. "That's why he's out in front. He's doing a job." Yasmin looked from the painting to the dog, then back, like she was checking his answer against the evidence, and grinned.

Mr. Chea gave them ten minutes to sketch anything in the station. Connor drew the old engine with its four horses and the small spotted shape leading them down a crowded street. It made him curious about what else a station needed around it, the whole little ecosystem of people, animals and machines that made a fire crew work. "I wonder what the dog's name was," he said. The firefighter passed by and tapped the brass plate under the painting. "Check the bottom of the frame," she said. Connor crouched down and read the small engraved letters: "Buster, 1898."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
Gabriel's kitchen smelled like burnt popcorn, and he was still arguing about it. "The popcorn burned because the microwave is haunted," he said, sliding the bowl across the counter to Carter. "That's just my opinion, so you can't say I'm wrong."

Carter poked at a black kernel. "Wait, that's not an opinion, though. That's a claim you can check." He pulled out his phone and typed while Gabriel groaned. "Watch. We test it. If the microwave is haunted, it would burn popcorn every time. If it's just old and weak, it burns it because the heat is uneven. Mr. Watanabe said something like that last week, about how some statements can be looked up."

"That's boring," said Elyana, coming in from the living room with a bag of unopened kernels. "But I want to see if it happens again, so keep going."

They ran three batches, one at a time, standing side by side and watching the bag spin. The first batch burned on the left side only. Carter turned the bag a quarter turn before the second batch, and the burn followed the same spot in the microwave, not the same side of the bag. "It's the microwave," he said. "The hot spot stays put. No ghost required."

"That's so weird," Elyana said, leaning closer to the glass door like she might catch the hot spot in the act. "You can't see it, but you can tell exactly where it is."

Gabriel still wasn't finished. "Fine, but the haunted thing was my opinion, and opinions can't be wrong. Like, I think the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin. That's my opinion."

Carter laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the bowl. "That's not an opinion, that's just a false claim. 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion. You can look it up. An opinion is like saying burned popcorn smells good, which, gross, but nobody can check it." He showed Gabriel the map on his phone, and Gabriel squinted at Paris like it had personally tricked him.

"Okay," Gabriel admitted. "So if I said my little brother is the loudest kid on the equator, that would be an opinion, but if I said he's taller than me, that's checkable."

"Exactly," said Carter. "Objective. Measurable. You get out a ruler and you know." He was already wondering what else they could test, because suddenly the whole house looked like a list of questions. "Hey, does your dad have any balloons? I want to see if the haunted hot spot can pop one."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days.
story:
Nolan had saved his question for the bus, because questions on the bus didn't count against the two he was allowed per field trip. "Why do pigs sit in mud?" he asked Austen, who was sharing his seat and most of his pretzels. Austen shrugged. "Because they're pigs. They like being gross." Emerald leaned over the aisle, holding her farm worksheet like evidence. "It says here to observe animal behavior, so maybe we should actually observe instead of guessing." Nolan stared out the window, where the heat shimmered above the road, and decided that "they like being gross" was the kind of answer that felt true but wasn't.

At the farm, the class reached the pig pen right after lunch, when the sun was at its worst. The pigs lay hip-deep in a brown wallow, completely still except for their ears. One pig near the fence wasn't in the mud at all; it stood in the shade, breathing fast. "That one's the anomaly," Nolan said, pointing. "All the others are in the muck, and that one isn't. If they just liked being dirty, why would one pig stay out?" Emerald scrutinized the pig in the shade, then the wallow, then the water trough beside it. "Maybe it's like the trough," she said slowly. "The mud is doing something the water does."

Nolan tested it. He hung back when the class moved on and watched the dry pig, and sure enough, when it finally waddled over, it went straight into the wallow and sank down with a grunt that sounded almost like relief. The farmer came by with a hose and grinned at the three of them lingering at the rail. "Smart, aren't they," she said. "Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days." Austen's mouth fell open. "They're not dirty," he said. "They're air conditioning themselves."

On the ride home, Emerald filled in her worksheet under "animal behavior," and Nolan added a line about the wallow, even though it wasn't required. He wasn't sure he'd get extra credit, but he wrote it anyway, in pen, so it felt permanent. "Next field trip," Austen said, tossing him the last pretzel, "you're asking more than two questions." Nolan caught it and ate it.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by using aluminum compounds that temporarily plug the sweat ducts.
story:
Alexandre noticed it first during dodgeball, when Eason waved him over and then leaned back a full step. "You smell like the gym lost a fight," Eason said, not meanly, but not quietly either. That was Tuesday. On Wednesday, Noelle slid her chair a few inches toward the window side of the desk they shared in Mr. Martínez's class, and Alexandre spent the rest of math staring at the poster about rainforest extinction instead of at his worksheet.

After school, his mom drove him to the pharmacy. "Get what you need," she said. "I'll wait in the car."

The deodorant shelf had two sticks from the same brand, nearly identical, in green and blue. Alexandre picked them both up and read the labels. One said deodorant. The other said antiperspirant. He read the backs twice. The green one's ingredient list included an aluminum compound; the blue one's did not.

A pharmacist restocking shampoo nearby glanced over. He looked about sixteen and bored. "Antiperspirant," Alexandre read aloud. "What's that word mean?"

"Antiperspirants reduce sweating by using aluminum compounds that temporarily plug the sweat ducts," the pharmacist said, then carried his box toward aisle four. Alexandre stood there holding both sticks. So the aluminum one plugged the ducts, the little tunnels the sweat came out of. The other one just covered the smell. He bought the green one with his allowance money.

The next morning he used it, then did a test. In science they were studying venomous animals, and Mr. Martínez had them run laps around the field to measure heart rates before and after. Alexandre ran hard, came inside, and checked the armpits of his shirt. Damp, but not soaked the way his shirt had been after dodgeball on Tuesday. He asked Noelle, without explaining why, whether she could smell anything from where she sat.

"Sharpie and rain," she said, sniffing. "That's the stick, right? It's fine. Way better than Tuesday."

At lunch, Eason asked where Alexandre had gotten the green stick, because Eason's older brother used some blue one that "doesn't do anything." Alexandre told him about the two labels, and Eason wanted proof. So they ran the fence line twice, came back, and compared shirts. Alexandre's was damp at the edges only. Eason's looked like he had swum across the creek with his clothes on.

"That's completely unfair," Eason said, peeling his shirt away from his chest.

"Trade me your chips and I'll tell you which one to buy," Alexandre said.

Eason looked at his chips, then at his shirt, and pushed the bag across the table.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Age-related hearing loss usually affects high-pitched sounds first, so voices can sound muffled even when they are loud enough.
story:
Abigail steered her grandfather past the tomato stall at the Saturday market, then watched it happen again. "Grandpa, Shreya's mom sells honey three rows down," she said, almost shouting. He leaned toward her, squinting, and asked, "What about money?" She had repeated herself all week, louder each time, and it never helped. The consequence was that he was starting to just nod at everything, and last night he had agreed, without hearing it, to attend her viola recital, which she hadn't even invited him to.

At the honey stall, Shreya's mother called out prices in her deep, carrying voice, and Grandpa answered every word, even the joke about bees. Abigail watched him laugh at the right moment, and a question formed. Her own voice was high. His hearing wasn't broken like a radio with the volume down; something was filtering it. She remembered Avah saying her grandmother complained that voices sounded muffled, mumbled, even when people spoke up. Loud enough, just smudged.

The market had a health booth with pamphlets, and Abigail picked one up while Grandpa examined jars. High tones go first, it said, so voices can sound muffled even when they're loud enough. She felt her face go warm, thinking of all the times she had practically yelled at him.

She tested it right there, dropping her voice low, almost like Shreya's mother. "Grandpa, my recital is Thursday. Do you actually want to come?"

He turned, and for once he didn't ask her to repeat it. "Thursday. I wouldn't miss it. Though you should know, I heard every word you said to Shreya on Tuesday about me being stubborn." His smile was sly. "Your friend's voice I can follow perfectly."

"So I'm the only one you can't hear?"

"Only the one I love most," he said, and paid for the honey.

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: A sauce that has turned lumpy can often be rescued by pushing it through a fine sieve or blending it smooth.
story:
The camp kitchen was a tarp roof and two propane burners, and tonight it belonged to Madison. Ms. Do had put her in charge of the cheese sauce for forty campers, which meant macaroni and cheese for the whole site, and Madison had practiced the roux exactly twice before today. She melted the butter in the pot, stirred in the flour, and watched it turn from white to pale gold, exactly the color the recipe card promised. Then she poured in the milk, added the cheese, and stirred, and for one shining moment the sauce looked smooth and competent, like something a real cook had made.

Then she turned away to check the pasta timer, and when she looked back, the sauce had begun to deteriorate. Lumps had risen all through it, pale blobs that clung to her spoon and refused to stir out. "No, no, no," she muttered, stirring harder, which only seemed to make more of them. Astrid leaned over her shoulder and winced. "That's not going on my noodles."

Madison stared into the pot and thought. The lumps had appeared after she stopped stirring, so leaving it alone was part of the trouble, but stirring now wasn't undoing anything. The flour and cheese must have grabbed onto each other while her back was turned, some hidden mechanism she couldn't see or reach with a spoon. If she couldn't break the lumps apart from inside the pot, maybe she could get them out of the pot entirely, or force them apart from outside. Princess, who was drying dishes beside her, held up a metal sieve. "We push the strawberries through this at home," she said. "Would it work on sauce?"

Madison set the sieve over a clean pot and poured. The sauce went through slowly, and she pressed the last stubborn lumps against the mesh with the back of her ladle until only a gritty smear remained behind. What came out the bottom was glossy and even, a proper cheese sauce with no lumps at all. "A sauce that's gone lumpy can be rescued by pushing it through a fine sieve," Madison said, almost to herself, filing the fact away. "Remember that."

The macaroni went into the big cooler to be portioned, and the line of campers formed in the lantern light. Astrid took the first bowl, twirled her fork, and held it up so the sauce ran off in one smooth ribbon. "Okay," she admitted, "I take back everything I said."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline that divides a picture into a three-by-three grid and places the main subject along those lines or where they cross.
story:
Lillian sat on the dock rail with her sketchbook open, glaring at her drawing of the estuary. All morning she had worked on it, because the camp was holding a photography and art showcase on Friday, and the best pieces would circulate on the big corkboard in the dining hall where everyone could see them. The drawing was accurate. The curved bank, the heron standing in the shallows, the water rippling out toward the sound. And it was completely boring.

"What's wrong with it?" Ronin asked, dropping onto the rail beside her with his sandwich. He chewed and looked. "The heron's good."

"The heron's fine. The whole thing is just... nothing." Lillian flipped back through her sketchbook to the postcard she'd bought at the camp store, a photo of the same estuary by some professional. Their herons were nearly identical. Their banks were nearly identical. But his picture pulled her eye somewhere and hers just sat there. She held the postcard up, then her drawing, then the postcard again.

Then she saw it. He hadn't put his heron in the middle. She grabbed her pencil and laid it across the postcard, then another pencil crosswise, dividing the photo into thirds each way, three rows and three columns. The heron stood almost exactly on one of the lines, right near a corner where two of the lines crossed. She did the same grid over her own drawing and there was her bird, dead center, with empty water spread flatly around it in every direction.

"That's a thing," Eileen said, leaning over from the other side. "My sister calls it the rule of thirds. You divide your picture into a three by three grid and put your main subject along those lines, or at the spots where they cross."

Lillian erased her stubborn, obstinate center marks and redrew the heron, shifted left, standing where a vertical third crossed a horizontal one. Suddenly the empty water wasn't empty anymore; it stretched off toward the corner like it was going somewhere. She left the foreground grasses crossing the lower third and let the horizon ride along the top line instead of slicing straight through the middle.

At the showcase on Friday, Ms. Cardinal stopped in front of Lillian's drawing for a long moment. "People will ask why this one works," she said. Lillian just smiled and pinned her two pencils back inside her sketchbook.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: The flutter kick in front crawl should come from the hips with fairly straight legs, since kicking mostly from the knees creates drag.
story:
Norah gripped the pool edge at the park's outdoor pool and watched the water churn under the afternoon sun. Twenty-five metres. That was the goal Mr. Harper had written on the whiteboard by the changerooms, and everyone in her group had to do front crawl with side breathing the whole way. She pushed off, flailed through ten metres, and grabbed the lane rope, gasping.

Julia floated over from the next lane, her cap slick as a seal's. "You kick like a stapler," she said. "All hinge and no push."

"Thanks a lot." Norah frowned at her own legs under the water. She had been kicking as hard as she could, knees bending and snapping, and still she barely moved. Something wasn't adding up. Effort in, no speed out. She looked down the lane at Mr. Harper's clipboard, then at a boy in lane four who was gliding past everyone with a lazy-looking kick, legs nearly straight, like his whole body was one long paddle. Norah chewed on that. Her kick came from her knees. His seemed to come from higher up, from his hips, like the movement started where his legs joined his body.

"I want to try something," she told Julia. She pushed off again, but this time she kept her legs fairly straight and let the kick roll out from her hips. It felt too easy, like she was barely trying, yet the tiles of the pool floor began sliding beneath her faster. One, two, breathe to the side. The far wall crept closer. She touched it and spun around, grinning so wide she swallowed a bit of water.

"I did fifteen!"

"Show me again," Julia said, already paddling to the edge. "My race is Saturday, and if that actually works, I need it too."

Norah took a breath and set off down the lane, hips rolling, legs sweeping long and straight beneath her like clockwork.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
The door opened before Lea's mom could knock, and a wall of cousins poured out into the hallway. Lea froze on the doormat. Aunt Sylvie grabbed her shoulders first and pressed her lips to Lea's right cheek, then her left. Two kisses. Then Uncle Bruno leaned in and did it three times, right, left, right, and Lea's face went hot because she had pulled back too early and his third kiss landed on air.

"Sorry," she mumbled.

"Do not be sorry," Uncle Bruno said, laughing. "In France we greet each other with cheek kisses. We call it la bise."

Inside, the apartment smelled of roasted chicken and something with cinnamon. Lea's mom had warned her about the kisses on the plane, but she had said nothing about the numbers. Two from Aunt Sylvie, who lived in Paris. Three from Uncle Bruno. Was it about age? Aunt Sylvie was older than Uncle Bruno, so that idea fell apart right away. Was it about how much they liked you? That thought intimidated Lea more than she wanted to admit, so she pushed it aside and decided to gather evidence instead.

At dinner, she watched. Little cousin Margot, who was eight, gave Grand-mère two kisses. But Grand-mère gave Margot three back, and Margot did not seem confused at all. Lea kept her napkin folded on her lap the way her mom had shown her, kept her wrists off the table because Uncle Bruno kept his elbows everywhere, and kept counting under her breath while pretending to eat her potatoes.

"Your bread goes on the table, not the plate," whispered the cousin from Lyon, who was twelve like Lea and had introduced herself as Céline an hour ago. Céline had spent the whole evening trying to get someone to play cards with her, and everyone kept saying after dinner. "Also, you are staring at everyone."

"I'm counting kisses," Lea whispered back. "Some people do two and some people do three."

Céline rolled her eyes like this was the most obvious thing in the world. "It depends where they come from. It is different in different regions. Maman is from Paris, so two. Papa's family is from the south, so three."

Lea sat back. It was a rule, like a hidden mechanism inside the family, and now she could see the whole pattern. She tested it on the next arrival, a great-aunt who swept in from Marseille. Three kisses, right on schedule. Lea grinned so wide that the great-aunt patted her cheek and asked what was so funny.

Later, when the plates were cleared and Céline still had no card partner, Lea dragged a chair over to the small table by the window. "Deal me in," she said. "But first, how many kisses do people give where you live?"

Céline leaned across the cards and kissed her twice, quick as shuffling. "Two. Now cut the deck."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
The smell of lemongrass and fried shallots drifted out onto the porch before Nevaeh even knocked. Jillian had promised that her grandmother's birthday dinner would be worth the bus ride across town, and Nevaeh, who had never been to a family gathering at anyone's house but her own, had spent the whole week quietly worrying about one thing: she did not want to look like a guest who didn't belong. Jillian's whole family would be there, uncles and cousins and a grandmother who had arrived from Jakarta only a month ago.

"Everyone's going to hug you," Jillian said at the door. "Even the ones you've never met. Fair warning." She was right. An uncle pressed Nevaeh's hand between both of his, a small cousin waved shyly from behind a chair, and Grandmother touched her own fingertips to her chest after Nevaeh said hello. Nevaeh noticed something else, too, something she couldn't quite name at first. When an aunt handed Grandmother a wrapped gift, she used her right hand. When Grandmother received it, she also used her right hand. When a cousin passed a plate of krupuk down the table, right hand again. Nevaeh kept watching, counting under her breath like she was collecting data for science class, and the pattern held every single time.

She tested a small idea. She passed the rice bowl with her left hand, casually, watching sideways. Grandmother's eyebrows lifted just a little, and she caught the bowl with her right hand and said something soft in Bahasa Indonesia to Jillian. Nevaeh's face went hot, but she made herself pay attention instead of shrinking into her chair. Maybe it wasn't rudeness she had committed. Maybe there was a rule, and rules could be learned.

"It's the right hand for eating and for giving and receiving things," Jillian whispered, leaning close. "In Indonesia and Malaysia. Grandma says it's a sign of respect." Nevaeh nodded and filed it away next to her observation, feeling oddly buoyant, as if the mistake had turned into something useful. She picked up her fork with her right hand, and when the birthday cake came around, she accepted her slice with both hands, right hand on top. Grandmother's face opened into a wide smile.

Later, while the cousins argued over the last piece of cake, Nevaeh had to confess something. "I passed the rice with my left hand on purpose," she told Jillian. "I was checking whether it was actually a rule or just a coincidence." Jillian laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her drink. "You ran an experiment at my grandma's birthday? She liked that, actually. She told my mom you paid attention." Grandmother appeared beside them just then and held out a small paper bag of sweets, offering it with her right hand. Nevaeh received it the same way, and Grandmother patted her gently on the head.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Eyeglass prescriptions measure lens strength in diopters, with a minus sign for nearsightedness and a plus sign for farsightedness.
story:
Elliot sat on the spinning chair in the eyeglass shop at the mall, holding his prescription slip like it was a report card. He had wanted glasses for a while, mostly because Sierra said he looked like a scientist in the try-on frames, but now the paper said -2.00 and his stomach dropped. Two days ago in science class he had gotten a minus on a quiz, and minus meant wrong.

"What's the face?" Sierra asked. She was leaning on the counter, eyeing the pretzel stand across the aisle, its butter smell drifting all the way over. "You got glasses. That's the best day of your life."

"It says negative two," Elliot said. "My eyes got a minus. Like they failed."

The optician, a woman with silver rings on every finger, laughed before she could stop herself. "No, no. That's not a score. It's the strength of the lens, measured in diopters." She tapped the slip. "Minus means nearsighted. Plus means farsighted. Yours is minus two, so things far away are blurry for you."

Elliot looked at the slip again. He turned it over, as if the back might hold more clues. Then he tested it, because testing things was what he did. He held the paper at arm's length, where it was sharp, then set it on the counter and stepped back three paces. The numbers went soft, like frost on the tundra photos in geography class, everything white and edgeless. So that was the pattern: near was clear, far was not. The minus wasn't a grade. The minus was just the direction his eyes leaned.

"So if Sierra needed glasses," he asked, "would hers say plus?"

"Only if she's farsighted," the optician said.

"Farsighted people can read the menu at the pretzel stand from here," Sierra said. "Nearsighted people like you need to walk over. It's basically a rule that I have to go get us both a cinnamon twist, since walking is prohibited for you now until your glasses are ready."

"That's not what nearsighted means," Elliot said, but he was grinning, and Sierra was already halfway across the aisle, coins counted out in her palm.

He tried on frames while he waited. The mirror showed a boy who did look a bit like a scientist, in a way that was entirely subjective and possibly influenced by the fact that Sierra had planted the idea weeks ago. The optician said his lenses would take twenty minutes. He watched the machine behind the counter grind the glass, a wheel of light spinning behind a little window, and he thought about the diopters again, the minus, the number that measured not failure but a direction.

"Order up," Sierra called, waving a pretzel at him from across the aisle. She took a bite of what was clearly the larger of the two.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: In a fire, smoke and heat rise, so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor, which is why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke.
story:
The bus doors hissed open at the nature reserve, and Audrey was first down the steps, notebook already in hand. Mr. Karimi had promised a visit to the fire station tucked behind the reserve's visitor centre, where firefighters would show how smoke behaved in a burning building. Audrey had been wondering about that all week. Why did the drills at school always say to crawl? Nobody ever said.

Inside the station, a firefighter set up a small demonstration room with a smoke machine, harmless haze curling from a vent near the ceiling. "Who wants to try crossing the room?" the firefighter asked. Marlee volunteered first and walked straight through, coughing and waving her hands even though the smoke wasn't real. Romy went next, same result, both of them laughing and rubbing their eyes.

Audrey stood at the doorway and watched instead. The haze hung high, drifting along the ceiling like a grey blanket, while the air near the floor stayed clear. She felt her curiosity sharpen into an idea. Maybe it wasn't just where the smoke happened to be; maybe it always gathered up there. She crouched low, then dropped to her hands and knees and crawled under the layer of grey. From down there she could see Marlee's sneakers and the whole clean strip of floor, cool and clear all the way to the far wall.

"Look at this!" she called, and Marlee and Romy dropped down beside her. "The smoke and heat go up," Audrey said, pointing at the ceiling. "The cleaner, cooler air is near the floor. That's why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke." Marlee crawled the length of the room twice, grinning, and Romy timed herself with the stopwatch from her backpack, like it was some kind of ritual.

Back outside on the reserve trail, the demonstration dissolved into ordinary sunshine and birdsong, but Audrey kept thinking about it. When they passed the marsh, she noticed mist floating above the water and wondered whether it moved the same way, buoyant and upward, before it vanished. She crouched at the boardwalk railing, watching the mist rise, and wrote one line in her notebook: the answer is almost always lower than you think. Then she scrambled up and jogged to catch the others.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: An introduction often opens with a hook, such as a question, a surprising fact or a short story, to catch the reader's interest before stating the thesis.
story:
The cafe smelled like cinnamon and burnt toast, and George had rewritten his first sentence four times. His essay was supposed to convince the school to start a recycling club, and Ms. Weber had written one word beside his opening paragraph: "Flat." He stared at the page so hard it was almost like he could scrutinize the letters themselves, hunting for whatever was missing.

Tomas slid into the booth across from him with a hot chocolate and peeked at the paper. "My opening was flat too," he said. "Araya fixed it."

"She did?" George remembered Araya's essay about the library staying open on Saturdays, the one she had read aloud in class. He had actually leaned forward in his seat when she started, and he hadn't even cared about libraries. Something about her first sentence had grabbed him and not let go.

Araya came back from the counter carrying a muffin, and before she even sat down George pushed the essay toward her. "How did you start yours?" he asked.

"With a hook," she said. "Like a question, or a surprising fact, or a tiny story. Something that catches the reader before you tell them your main idea." She pulled the essay closer and read his first line: "Our school should have a recycling club for several important reasons." Then she grabbed a napkin and a pen. "Let's test three."

Tomas counted them off on his fingers. "One, his boring one. Two, a question." Araya wrote, "Did you know our school throws away hundreds of bottles every week?" George frowned. He wasn't sure the number was exact. "Make it approximate," he said, and she added the word "about" so the sentence stayed honest. "Three, a story," Tomas said, so George tried, "Last Tuesday I watched a kid toss a whole water bottle into the trash can right beside the recycling bin."

Then they did the experiment. Araya read each opening out loud in a flat, robot voice, and George closed his eyes and paid attention to his own attention. The first one made his mind drift to the window. The question made him wonder, just a little. The little story made a picture pop into his head, sharp and clear, like one neuron lighting up a whole string of others. "That one," he said, pointing at the napkin. "Definitely that one."

He copied the sentence onto his paper, then crossed it out and wrote it again, changing Tuesday to Friday because that was the day it had really happened. Ms. Weber had said to begin with the truth, even the small truths. He thought about his flat first try and felt a little embarrassed, but also strange and pleased, the way you do when a locked door finally swings open. Tomas stole a corner of his muffin, and Araya said, "Read the whole thing now, robot voice," so George squared his shoulders and began, "Last Friday I watched a kid toss a whole water bottle into the trash can right beside the recycling bin."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The terminator is the line on a sphere where the lit side turns into the shadow side, the edge where direct light stops reaching.
story:
Lucy had signed up for the pottery shed at Camp Winnowood mostly because Cohen said the kiln smelled like burnt cookies, but the moment she sat down at the drawing table, she wanted in. Ms. Sok had set a plaster ball on a cloth with a single lamp beside it, and every kid in the room was leaning forward.

"Today we shade a sphere," Ms. Sok said. "Highlight, shadow, cast shadow. And one more thing to find, if you can."

"A robot part?" Cohen whispered.

"Terminator," Remi whispered back, and Lucy laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water cup. Ms. Sok only smiled and said the word was real, and that they would have to figure out what it meant on their own.

Lucy squinted at the ball. The lamp made one bright spot, the highlight, and the side away from the lamp went dark. Her pencil guessed at where the light stopped reaching. She drew a curved line and shaded everything past it. Remi leaned over. "Too far back," she said. "See? The gray part starts here." Lucy looked again, and she could see it, a curving edge on the ball where the lit side turned into the shadow side, where the direct light stopped reaching. She pressed her thumb along the ball's surface to feel the spot go cold and warm, as if her skin could confirm what her eyes already knew. "The terminator," she said quietly, trying the word out, and this time nobody laughed, because they were all hunting for it on their own drawings.

Lucy decided to test her idea. She slid the lamp slowly around the table and watched the terminator crawl across the plaster like something alive, the whole shadow side turning with it, while the dark oval on the cloth, the cast shadow, swung away like a door. She tried it three times to be sure. When Ms. Sok passed by, Lucy spun the sketchbook toward her, finger on the line. "It moves with the light," Lucy said. "Wherever the light goes, that's where the lit side stops."

Ms. Sok gave a nod, the kind Lucy recognized from when someone got it exactly right. "Keep going," she said. "Next week, contemporary portraits, and you'll need this." Lucy bent back over the sphere, compressed the whole night down to one curved pencil line, and beside her Cohen drew a tiny robot, just to be safe.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right.
story:
The bus to the regional bee took forty minutes, and Mr. Silva had brought a box of index cards to fill every one of them. "Practice round," he said, standing at the front while the driver pulled out of the school lot. "Autumn and Wren, you're our two regional spellers. Spell against each other. Loser buys the winner a pretzel at the venue."

Autumn slid into a seat near the middle, and Elisha sat down beside her. Autumn had spent three weeks hoping Wren would catch the flu, or trip over a dictionary, or spell one word wrong. Second place meant you watched someone else hold the trophy. She had decided it would be unbearable.

Wren took the seat across the aisle. "Ready?" he asked.

"Not really," Autumn said, which was true.

Mr. Silva held up the first card. "Sustain. Autumn."

"S-U-S-T-A-I-N. Sustain."

"Correct. Wren, brittle."

"B-R-I-T-T-L-E. Brittle."

"Correct."

They went through twelve words that way, then twenty. Every card, both of them, no mistakes. Elisha kept score on the back of her notebook and after a while stopped writing anything at all, because there was nothing to write. The bus hummed, the cards kept coming, and nobody got a word wrong.

Elisha leaned over the notebook. "You know what happened at the real Nationals? The 2019 Scripps bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight winners. They just ran out of words before anyone missed."

"Eight?" Autumn said.

"Eight. Sharing the title."

Autumn looked at the stack of cards in Mr. Silva's hand. She had been thinking about the bee all wrong, like it was a wall with room for only one person on top. But if eight spellers could each get every word right, then the wall had more room than she had imagined. If she and Wren both spelled perfectly, neither of them had to lose. She turned to the aisle.

"Wren," she said, "what if we both just keep going until the cards run out?"

"Then we both get pretzels," Wren said, "and we each buy our own."

"That works too."

Mr. Silva shuffled the deck once more. "Privilege," he said. "Autumn."

"P-R-I-V-I-L-E-G-E. Privilege."

"Correct. Wren, crescendo."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates exactly twice as fast, which is why the two sound like the same note at different heights.
story:
The choir room at the concert hall smelled like dust and old velvet, and Ryan stood between Shea and Yanis holding his folder like a shield. Mr. Hassan had split them into two groups, and Ryan's group had to sing the lower line while the other group held the higher one. The trouble started the moment both groups sang at once. Ryan kept drifting upward, sliding into the other part like a paper boat pulled along by a current.

"You're doing it again," Shea whispered after the third crash of sound. "You follow whoever is loudest."

Ryan frowned. He wasn't doing it on purpose. It felt almost like gravity. "Why does the high part drag me up like that?" he asked. Yanis shrugged, but Ryan kept turning the question over in his mind while Mr. Hassan played the two lines on the piano, one after the other. Something about them nagged at him. They clashed when they were wrong, but when they were right, the high line sounded strangely familiar, almost like his own line wearing a taller hat.

At break, Ryan dragged Shea to the piano and played the low note, then the note an octave up. "Sing this one," he said, pointing at the low key. Shea sang it. "Now this one." Shea sang the high one. Ryan's eyes went wide. "They're the same note," he said slowly. "It's like the same note, just higher. An octave, Mr. Hassan called it. So when I hear the other part, it sounds so much like mine that my brain grabs it and climbs." He wondered if the note's sound was somehow doubling on its way up, and he tested it in his head, humming the low note and feeling how the high one seemed to fit inside it, a smaller copy of the same thing.

Back in formation, Ryan tried a new trick. Every time the high part floated near, he pictured his own note as the floor and their note as the ceiling directly above it, same shape, different height. When the two groups sang together, his voice stayed put. The low line held steady, warm and solid, and the high line shimmered over top of it. For the first time, the sound wasn't a crash. It was a chord, the kind that made the hair on his arms stand up.

Mr. Hassan lowered his hands and grinned at them. "Whatever you just did," he said, "do it again at the concert."

Ryan felt an idea begin to germinate, a whole plan taking root. "Saturday," he whispered to Shea, "I'm going to write a memoir about this. Chapter one: how I stopped floating."

Shea laughed. "Chapter two: how you started bragging."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Regression to the mean means unusually bad days tend to be followed by more ordinary ones, so people who try a remedy when symptoms are worst may improve even if it does nothing.
story:
Juliette found the ginger tea on the clearance shelf, one box left, an endangered supply if her grandmother had anything to say about it. Grandma was two aisles over comparing cough drops, and Juliette held the box while a woman nearby grabbed three boxes of some purple headache powder and hurried to the register like it was the last lifeboat. At the counter, Mr. Bakker rang her up without a word about miracles. That was the strange part, Juliette thought. If the purple powder worked so well, why was it on clearance?

Grandma had sworn by the tea since Tuesday. Her headache that day had been the worst in months, she said, and by Wednesday morning it was nearly gone. "One cup," she kept repeating as Juliette carried the box toward the front. "That's all it took." Juliette wanted to believe her, but something nagged at her, a small contradiction she couldn't put her finger on. Grandma's headaches came and went anyway, didn't they? Hadn't there been bad ones back in October, before any tea? At the register Juliette set down the box and pulled a receipt from her pocket, blank side up, and began to draft a chart right there, a column for every bad-headache day she could remember and what came after. Mr. Bakker watched her scribble without interrupting.

"You're blocking my register," said a voice behind her. It was Danica from science class, holding cold medicine for her mom. Juliette stepped aside but kept writing. The pattern was there, and it made her stomach tighten. The worst days, the ones Grandma called unbearable, were always followed by ordinary days. Tea or no tea. Even back in October. Even the time in July when Grandma had tried a heating pad instead.

"It's a real thing," Danica said, peering over her shoulder. "Regression to the mean. Worst days drift back toward normal on their own." Juliette stared at her lopsided columns, torn between disappointment and the odd thrill of having caught something invisible in the act.

She bought the tea anyway. "For the taste," she told Grandma, sliding the bag across the seat of the car. "And maybe next bad headache, we time it."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
story:
Evan slid his flashcards across the library table and checked the clock above the biography shelves. Twenty minutes until he had to stand up in front of Ms. Li's class and describe his family in Spanish, using full sentences, no single words allowed.

Roger leaned over the cards. "You've got nine sentences. That's plenty."

"It's not the number," Evan said. "Something's wrong with one of them, and I can't find it." He had copied his sentences from his notebook, where his notes had started as a whole page and slowly condensed into neat cards, one per family member. His dog was obstinate, which he'd written as "terco." His mother was a nurse. His grandfather was tall. And his brother was tired, because Hugo had stayed up all night finishing a model bridge.

Kennery dropped into the chair across from them, out of breath. "Ms. Li says start in the corner by the atlas stand," she said. Then she squinted at the cards. "Why does Hugo get two cards?"

He didn't. Evan counted. There was "Mi hermano es alto," from his grandfather's card somehow copied wrong, and "Mi hermano está cansado." He stared at the two little verbs, es and está, which he had been treating as the same word all week. He flipped through his cards and found the same pair again: "Mi madre es enfermera" but "Mi perro está en el sótano." His dog was not permanently in the basement. His dog went outside constantly, tracking mud, chewing the mail. So why would the same English word, is, come out two different ways?

"Roger," Evan said slowly, "say 'my brother is tall' in Spanish."

"Mi hermano es alto. Obviously."

"Now say 'my brother is tired.'"

Roger opened his mouth, then stopped. He looked at the cards, then at Evan, and the room got quiet enough that they could hear the radiator ticking.

Evan tested his idea on the safest card he had, the one about Hugo. If es meant lasting things, like being tall, then saying "Mi hermano es cansado" would mean his brother was tired forever, permanently wiped out, a boy doomed to yawn through every birthday for the rest of his life. And if está was for right now, then his tired-brother card should use está, and it already did. He checked the rest of the stack card by card, pencil hovering.

Kennedy pointed at the grandfather card, the one Evan had botched. "Es alto," she said. "Lasting. That one's safe."

"Ser for what lasts," Roger said, tapping the tall card. "Estar for right now."

Evan scratched out one verb, wrote the other, and squared the cards into a clean stack just as Ms. Li appeared at the end of the aisle.

"Mr. Alvarez," she said. "You're first."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen every two hours outdoors, and immediately after swimming or sweating.
story:
Hunter's grandmother lived three streets from the beach, and the whole family had come down for the long weekend. On Saturday morning his mother slathered sunscreen on his shoulders before he and his cousin Alexia went out to fly kites on the sand. They stayed out until lunch, running back and forth until the kite string hummed.

After sandwiches, Alexia begged to go swimming, and they spent the whole afternoon in the water, diving under waves until their fingers wrinkled. Nobody mentioned sunscreen again. By dinnertime Hunter's back felt tight, and when his grandmother turned him toward the kitchen light, she clicked her tongue. His shoulders were red.

"That's a burn," she said. "You put cream on this morning, didn't you?"

"A whole lot of it," Hunter said. He sat on the counter while she fetched the aloe.

He thought about the timeline while she dabbed it on. He'd been outside for hours, and he'd been in the water for more hours after that. Alexia, sitting on the stairs with her own pink nose, was doing the same math. "Maybe it wears off," she said slowly. "Like, after a while?"

Hunter wanted to test it, but not with another burn. On Sunday he set a timer on his phone before they went out, and when it buzzed at two hours he made everyone stop and put on more cream. They swam after lunch, and the moment they climbed out and toweled off, he called them back to the beach bag for another round. Alexia groaned but held out her arms.

"The things I do for science," she said.

His rebellious little brother tried to run off without any, and Hunter chased him down and got the back of his neck. Their grandmother watched from her chair, saying nothing, just raising her glass of lemonade.

That evening Hunter stood in front of the hallway mirror, twisting to see his shoulders. They were the same color as morning, not a trace of red. He snapped a photo of the timer screen and set a new alarm for tomorrow.

"Ten a.m., beach," he told Alexia. "Bring the bag."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
story:
The group chat pinged at 7:14 on a Tuesday evening, while Hannah was watching rain slide down her bedroom window. Abdullah had posted, all capitals: THE SCHOOL IS CLOSING THE WALK TRAIL BEHIND THE FIELD ON MONDAY. Channing answered with three exclamation points. Hannah read the message twice, then a third time, because Monday was the day she and Abdullah walked that trail to the corner store for licorice.

She remembered Ms. Holloway's classroom in September, the tranquil afternoon light on the whiteboard, when a girl named Priya had argued for a crosswalk on Marsh Road. Priya had counted near-misses, actual moments when cars braked hard for kids, and stood at the front saying, "It's my opinion we need a crosswalk, and I counted fourteen near-misses in one week to back it up." Ms. Holloway had written on the board: an opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons. Hannah had copied it into her notebook, and now those words floated back to her like a message in a bottle.

Abdullah's post, she noticed, was only an opinion shaped like a fact. It had no evidence attached at all, no photo, no memo, no reason.

She typed: "Where did you hear that?" Then she set the phone face down on her quilt and made a plan. If the trail were really closing, there would be a sign. Signs had to go up before Monday, because that was how the school did things. She pulled on her rain boots and walked the three blocks through drizzle, past the tranquil pond where the ducks tucked their heads under their wings.

The trail gate stood open, wet and ordinary. No sign. No tape. She took a photo and walked home.

In the chat she posted the picture with the caption "Trail looks fine. Anybody see an actual notice?" Abdullah went quiet for four whole minutes, the little typing bubble appearing and vanishing. Then he wrote: "ok it was just something my cousin said. i thought it sounded true." Channing sent a single laughing face.

Hannah smiled at her screen. "Your cousin can have opinions," she typed. "But next time bring evidence." Then, because a thought was still nagging her, she added one more message: "Also, did anyone check if the store is even open Monday?" Abdullah answered fastest this time: "IT CLOSES AT SIX. MY COUSIN WORKS THERE. I ASKED HIM DIRECTLY."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and sweat, and Mr. Ahmadi had looped a thick rope across the center line for the last drill of practice. "Six on each side," he called. "Pull." Alexandre gripped the rope beside Alisa and Abbie and hauled until his shoulders burned, but the rope barely moved, and neither did the other team's. Afterward Mr. Ahmadi shook his head. "Some of you are easing off. I can feel it in the rope."

That evening Alexandre pulled his library book on sports science off the shelf and read until he found it. In 1913, Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller. He read the sentence twice. So it wasn't just his team being lazy, and it wasn't just the coach imagining things. The bigger the group, the less each person pulled on average. He needed to see it for himself.

At the next practice he asked Alisa to help him after the whistle. First she pulled the rope alone, dragging a stack of folded mats, and he marked the distance with tape. Then they pulled together, both hands on the rope, and the mats moved again. Alexandre measured with a tape measure and did the arithmetic on his palm with a pencil stub. Alisa's share was smaller when they pulled together. He ran it again with Abbie added, and it shrank again. "It happens every time," he told them. "More people, smaller pull from each."

Before Friday's meet, Alexandre told Mr. Ahmadi he wanted shorter pulls with fewer players rotating in, so nobody drifted half-hearted on a long rope. Mr. Ahmadi tried it. In the gymnasium the crowd of parents, tenants of the bleachers who paid nothing but cheered loudly, went quiet as the rope crept across the line. The knot, durable and tight, slapped down on their side of the tape.

Abbie pounded his shoulder. "Told you the math kid would figure it out."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil that producers use again.
story:
Chase spread his poster board across the kitchen table and stared at the empty page. The assignment was due tomorrow: draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, and then explain what happens if one link disappears. He had the sun part easy. He even liked drawing the sun, a big blazing circle with arrows shooting out like the whole picture would orbit around it. But after that, his chain wobbled. Grass, then a rabbit, then a fox. Done in three minutes. It felt too short, too simple, and he couldn't figure out what he was missing.

"Where does it all go when things die?" he muttered, chewing his pencil. "Foxes don't live forever."

The doorbell rang. It was Maisie, holding a plastic bag with half a rotten apple in it, because Maisie was like that. "Science emergency too?" she asked. Chase showed her his poster. She frowned at it, then pointed at the apple. "See this gross part? There's fuzz on it. My grandpa calls them decomposers." She peeled the bag open. "Decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals. Then the nutrients go back into the soil, and plants use them again."

Chase sat up so fast his chair scraped. That was the missing loop. The grass at the start of his chain wasn't just sitting there; it was pulling nutrients out of soil that dead foxes and rabbits had helped make. "So the chain isn't a straight line," he said slowly, drawing a curved arrow from the fox all the way back around to the grass. "It's a circle. The end feeds the beginning."

"Test it," Maisie said, defiant against his doubt, pointing at his last empty box. "Cross out the decomposers and see what breaks." Chase drew an X through his loop. No nutrients going back to the soil meant weaker grass, fewer rabbits, hungrier foxes. The whole chain went gray. He erased the X, colored the loop in bold green, and added a small note about water rising as vapor into clouds that would rain on the grass again, because the sun really did run everything.

The next morning he carried the poster to school like a shield. Mr. Zhang looked at the curved arrow for a long moment, then pinned the poster to the wall at the very front of the room.

"Class," he said, tapping the loop with one finger. "Start here."

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking.
story:
Rosalie stood at Noemie's kitchen counter with a wooden spoon in her hand and a pot of pale, lumpy paste in front of her. The lumps looked like tiny wet dumplings, and every time she stirred, more of them appeared.

"Grandma arrives at six," Noemie said, checking the clock for the third time. "She's French. She'll take one bite and know." Noemie's whole plan for the visit was this dinner, homemade mac and cheese, and now her plan was sitting in the pot looking like a science experiment.

Rosalie frowned at the lumps. They had followed the recipe on Noemie's phone exactly, butter, then flour, then milk, then cheese. So why lumps? She thought about the order of things. The flour had glued itself into little balls the second the milk hit it. Maybe the milk was the problem, not the flour. Maybe it had to go in slowly, so slow the flour didn't have a chance to clump. She scraped the lumpy pot into a bowl and started over.

This time she melted the butter, whisked in the flour, and let it bubble until it smelled like toasted nuts. Then she poured the warm milk in a thin stream with one hand while whisking hard with the other. Her first pour was hesitant, just a dribble, but the sauce stayed smooth, so she poured faster. Within a minute the pot held glossy, velvety sauce. She stirred in the cheese and it melted into a golden ribbon.

Noemie's little brother Eli wandered in and stuck a finger toward the pot. "Your hands are shaking," he said. "It's probably hormones."

"It's probably whisking," Rosalie said, and Noemie laughed so hard she snorted.

From the back fence, Ms. Mercado, the neighbour who traded tomatoes for cookies, called through the window. "That smells like a proper roux. Where did you two learn that?"

"The internet," Rosalie admitted. "But we didn't know it had a name."

"A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel," Ms. Mercado said, "one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking."

Noemie's eyes went wide. "Mother sauces. Grandma is going to be so impressed." Then she paused. "Wait. My birthday is Thursday, and Grandma's visit almost coincides with it, so technically this could count as birthday dinner too."

"That's cheating," said Eli.

"That's efficiency," said Noemie, and she spooned the sauce over the noodles while Rosalie held the pot steady, both of them grinning as the golden sauce ran down in a smooth, unbroken stream.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
story:
Violet stood at her grandmother's grave with an empty stomach and a head full of questions. The fast had started at sunset yesterday, and now it was late afternoon, and the horizon was refusing to do anything interesting. She scrutinized the sky above the cemetery fence as if staring could push the sun down faster, which she knew was vain, but she did it anyway.

"Still not eating?" Callum asked. He had biked here to meet her, munching crackers from his pocket, which Violet thought was practically cheating.

"It's not just not eating," she said. "It's a whole day. My mom says it's from sunset yesterday until after nightfall tonight." She counted on her fingers. "That's not twenty-four hours. It's about twenty-five."

"Why the extra hour?"

"I don't know yet. Nobody would just tell me, so I'm figuring it out." She pulled her jacket tighter. The air smelled of cut grass and cold stone, and somewhere a crow argued with itself.

Mr. Vu was there too, watering the mums he planted beside his wife's headstone every September. Last year, on this same day, Violet had been home with a fever, swallowing spoonfuls of the pink antibiotic that sat in the refrigerator door, while her parents came here without her. She had cried about it at the time, sick and left out, and she still wasn't sure whether the crying had been about missing her grandmother or about being left behind. Both, probably.

Tonight she was trying the whole thing for the first time, fast and all, and she had a theory. If it ended only after nightfall, and not just at sunset, then maybe the day wasn't measured by the sun alone. She watched the sky deepen from gold to gray to a blue so dark it was almost black, and when the first stars came out she held up her hand and counted three.

"Okay," she said. "Now."

Her mother unwrapped the apples and honey, and Violet bit down.

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: Python variable names are case-sensitive, so Number and number are two different variables.
story:
Anna typed the loop for the third time and ran it, certain this attempt would work. On the screen, in red letters, appeared the same message as before: NameError: name 'number' is not defined.

"I don't get it," she said, pulling her sleeves down over her hands the way she did when she was thinking hard. "The variable is right there."

Kinsley leaned over from the kitchen chair beside her, chewing the last of an apple. "You named it in the input line, right? Copy it to me."

Anna read aloud, pointing at each word. "Number equals input, times equals int, then for i in range one to thirteen, print Number times i."

Kinsley frowned. "Wait. Say the first part again."

"Number capital N, equals input, 'Which times table?'"

"And in the print?"

Anna looked. "number, small n." Her stomach did a strange little flip, the same feeling as stepping onto the last stair and finding nothing under her foot. Could one letter really break everything?

"Try this," Kinsley said. "Make them match. Capital in both places."

Anna's fingers seemed to contract as she hovered over the keys, then she changed the print line to capital Number and hit run. She held her breath. Instead of red, white text scrolled up the screen: 7, 14, 21, all the way to 84, marching down in a straight column.

"It worked," Anna whispered. She typed 9 in the input box and ran it again, and the nines marched down too. She sat back so fast the chair squeaked. "Number and number are two different variables. Python sees them as two names."

Kinsley dropped her apple core in the bowl. "One capital letter."

"One capital letter," Anna said, and deleted the whole program so she could build it again from scratch, this time watching every n.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: The voice comes from two vocal folds in the larynx that vibrate as air passes between them; tightening them raises the pitch.
story:
Clara had turned her grandpa's garage into a rehearsal studio, with a folding table for a stage and an old paint bucket for a drum. On Saturday Farrah arrived carrying sheet music, and behind her came Jannah, who was skeptical that two people could sing different notes at the same time and not sound like a broken doorbell. "Mr. Weiss says the whole choir has to hold our part while the other part tries to pull us off," Clara said, bouncing on her toes. "If we can do it in here, we can do it anywhere."

They started on the low line, the one Clara had been assigned, and it went fine until Farrah slid up to her high notes. Clara's voice drifted upward after it, like a balloon on a string, and suddenly they were both singing the same wrong note. "It's like my throat follows yours," Clara said. She touched her neck and frowned. Something in there was doing this. She remembered the choir booklet Mr. Weiss had left on the piano bench, and she ran inside to fetch it, skidding back on the concrete in her socks.

The booklet had a diagram. Two vocal folds in the larynx, it said, vibrate as air passes between them, and tightening them raises the pitch. "So when I chase your note, I'm tightening," Clara said, feeling her throat. "The folds squeeze higher. If I keep them loose, I stay low." Jannah looked skeptical, but Farrah grinned. "Test it. Sing your note, and I'll sneak mine in."

Clara held her note like a rope in a tug of war, keeping her throat loose and heavy while Farrah's high part floated above it. For three whole bars they were two notes at once, and it sounded, Farrah shouted, like an actual choir. Then came the twist: the low note wasn't Clara's note at all. When they checked the music, the low line belonged to Jannah, who had been quietly mouthing along. Jannah shrugged. "I didn't want to elaborate on it before, but I've been practicing in my room for weeks." They all shrieked, and Clara dragged the paint bucket over. "Okay, new plan. Jannah low, me high, Farrah in the middle. From the top."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Cats cannot make enough of their own taurine, a nutrient found in meat, and a lack of it can cause heart disease and blindness.
story:
The kitten rode home in a cardboard box with holes punched in the sides, and Avery kept her palm flat against the lid the whole way so it wouldn't slide.
