His name was Biscuit, and he was hers, which meant she was the one who had to figure out what he needed. The shelter had given her a bag of food, but it was almost empty, and her dad had said, "We'll grab more at the store tomorrow."

At the pet store, Avery's classmate Yassin was there buying dog food for his labrador. He looked at the shelf with her and frowned. "Why do they even make them separate? Food is food, isn't it?" That was exactly what Avery had been wondering, so she turned over a can of dog food and a can of cat food and compared the labels. The lists weren't the same. The cat food had something the dog food didn't. "Taurine," she read aloud, and a cashier nearby said, "You want that in cat food, trust me," and walked off before Avery could ask why.

She wasn't going to guess. Biscuit was too small to be an experiment. At home she looked it up and found something that surprised her: cats can't make enough taurine on their own, and it comes from meat. She read further, and the next part made her sit back. If a cat doesn't get enough, it can end up with heart disease, or even go blind. No wonder the dog food excluded it; dogs didn't need it added the same way. She checked the shelter's bag, and sure enough, taurine was on the label, near the top. She wrote it on the shopping list in capital letters so nobody would come home with the wrong bag.

The next morning Louise came over to meet Biscuit. He had climbed the curtain and gotten stuck halfway up, and he meowed down at them like it was their fault. "He eats better than I do," Louise said, watching Avery measure out his breakfast. Biscuit smelled the bowl, jumped off the curtain rail, and landed with a thump right in the middle of the kibble.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood.
story:
Emily had tried to conceal the problem for weeks, squinting at the board and copying Jorja's notes, but on Friday Mr. Chea caught her guessing at the homework questions written behind him. On Monday she walked into class with a new pair of glasses, purple at the corners, and the board jumped out at her all at once, every letter sharp as a cutout. Jorja leaned over during silent reading. "They look good," she whispered. "Can you see everything now?"

"Even the back wall," Emily whispered back. "The clock says 9:42." She could also see the pamphlet the eye doctor had given her mother, folded into her backpack, and at recess she pulled it out under the old maple at the corner of the yard, where the leaves were still lush and green. One sentence stopped her: studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood. She read it twice. Near sighted. That was her. She thought about her weekends, Saturday and Sunday, screen after screen, curtains shut against the glare.

Aedan kicked a pinecone across the grass. "What are you staring at?"

"This says nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood," Emily said. "All of it. When they were kids." She looked up. "You're outside all the time. Soccer, hiking, everything."

"So?"

"So your eyes had a better chance than mine did. My weekends were all screens." She stood and brushed off her jeans. "I want to test something. This weekend, no screens. Outside, both days, as much as I can stand. I don't think it'll fix my glasses, but I want to see what it's like."

On Saturday morning Emily dragged Aedan and Jorja to the creek trail before anyone could invent an excuse. They caught tadpoles in a jar, lost the jar, found it again downstream, and ate sandwiches on a flat rock that Jorja declared was probably a hundred years old. Emily's legs ached and her socks were soaked, but when the sun slanted low she realized she had not thought about a screen since breakfast. On Sunday they came back, and on Monday Mr. Chea was waiting by the door with a box of seedlings. "Community garden plot," he said. "I'm retiring at the end of the year, and once my pension starts I won't be around to water these, so somebody had better learn."

Emily raised her hand so fast her glasses slid down her nose. She pushed them up and said, "Every day after school. Outside counts."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Megan was lying on her bed with her tablet, half in the science-club group chat and half in a search engine, when she typed her own name just to see what would happen. Up came a comment she'd written two years ago on a fan site for a show she didn't even watch anymore. It had her full name attached, right there, like a fossil nobody had asked to keep.

She screenshotted it and dropped it in the chat. "Um. Why is this here? I posted this forever ago."

Braelynn replied with three surprised emojis. "That's so weird. I thought stuff disappeared when you stopped going on a site."

"It doesn't," Talon typed. "My cousin says search engines have automated programs called crawlers that copy and index public pages. That's how old stuff turns up in search results." His next message appeared before she could answer. "Also, urgent topic: my objective for this weekend is to get everyone to come to the creek cleanup, and I need one more person or Mr. Nikolaidis says the club can't reserve the pavilion."

Megan stared at the screenshot again. "So if my comment is public, a crawler copied it? Like a little robot reading everything and saving it?" She thought of the photo she'd posted last month with the school sign in the background, the one that showed exactly where she'd be every Tuesday after school. Her stomach did a slow flip.

She tried an experiment. She searched Braelynn's username, then her own, then a fake name she made up on the spot. Only the fake name came back empty. "Okay, tested it. Anything public with your real name on it can show up. Anything with a made-up name, nothing."

"That contradicts everything I believed about the delete button," Braelynn wrote.

"Delete is frail," Megan typed. "Public is forever, apparently."

Talon sent a single pleading message: "CREEK. PAVILION. SATURDAY."

"Fine," Megan wrote back, "but I'm deleting my location posts first." She opened her photo settings and got to work.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: A warm-up of light jogging and moving stretches raises heart rate and muscle temperature, which helps muscles work better before a hard effort.
story:
Rosalie bounced on her toes at the edge of the running track, her shoelaces double-knotted and her hair pinned back for speed. Tryouts for the school relay team started in ten minutes, and she wanted one of those four spots more than she wanted her birthday. Loic was already jogging the curved path by the bleachers, swinging his arms in wide, easy circles, and Daniel was doing walking lunges that made him look like a giant, cheerful insect.

"Come watch with me," said a girl from her class, perched on the lowest bleacher step. "I don't want to waste energy before we run. I'm too nervous anyway." Rosalie almost sat down. Then she noticed something: every kid who had jogged even one slow lap was breathing faster, cheeks pink, and when they stretched they kept moving, never holding still. Mr. Sultani strolled past the bleachers, humming, and called out, "Keep those knees warm, people, be kind to your cartilage," without stopping.

Rosalie thought about her legs like an engine. A slow jog and moving stretches get your heart pumping faster and your muscles warmer, and warm muscles work better when you ask them for something hard. That was what her legs felt like on cold mornings: stiff and slow until she'd run around the yard once. So she tested it. "Race you one easy lap," she said to Loic, and they jogged it together, then did Daniel's funny lunges plus high knees. Her heart was beating quicker now, her legs loose and ready, and she hadn't spent anything she needed.

The whistle blew. The girl on the bleacher, who had only watched, shot off the line fast, then faltered halfway down the backstretch, her steps turning heavy. Rosalie passed her, arms pumping, and crossed the line second behind Daniel, whooping. Loic raised both fists. Later, when the coach posted the relay list, Rosalie's name sat in the third slot, and she ran to show Loic, waving the paper over her head like a flag.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
story:
Clara stood in the pharmacy aisle staring at two boxes of anti-itch cream, because her little brother's mosquito bites had turned him into a human scratch machine and their mom would be back from the register in fifteen minutes. The first box showed a lush green meadow and a woman smiling, with a quote that read, "It worked for me in one day!" The second box was plain, with small print that said 300 people had tested it in a lab.

Dorian leaned over her shoulder. "Get the meadow one. My cousin used it and her bites cleared right up."

"That's one cousin," Clara said. She flipped the plain box over and read further. "This one had three hundred people try it." Rowan, who had tagged along to buy bandages for his skateboard elbows, shook his head.

"Three hundred strangers versus a cousin you actually know," he said. "I trust the cousin."

Clara thought about the class survey last week, when Mr. Do had asked three kids if they loved the cafeteria's fish sticks and all three said yes, and then the whole school voted and only forty kids out of two hundred did. She had laughed about it with Mr. Do at the time, and now something clicked. "Three people can all love something by accident," she said slowly. "Two hundred people can't all be that weird."

"So bigger groups are more reliable," Rowan said.

"Because the weird ones even out," Clara said. "Dorian's cousin might just have tough skin."

Dorian frowned. "Then why do companies print the cousin-style quotes at all?"

"Because they're cheap to get, I bet." Clara put the plain box in the basket, then hesitated. "But my brother has sensitive skin. The small print warns it might irritate some people." She carried both boxes to the counter, where Mr. Do was waiting behind the register, and slid them toward him.

"Which one would you trust for a kid with sensitive skin?" she asked. "The one with the smiling lady, or the one with the three hundred testers?"

Mr. Do tapped the plain box twice. "That one."

Clara put the meadow box back on the shelf herself.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
story:
Lucas slid into the last seat on the bus and realized Dania was already there, hood up, staring at the window. They had not really talked since October, when he joined the soccer team and she joined debate, and the space between them had grown like something with its own schedule.

"Mr. Pham made us read a study today," Lucas said, because silence was worse than awkwardness. "From 2015. It followed 573 friendships that started in seventh grade." Dania's hood tilted a fraction, which he took as a signal to keep going. "Friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end." He had copied it onto his palm during class, as if he might need proof later, and now he did. "So I guess that's us. You do debate, I do soccer. Less alike every week."

"We were alike in sixth grade," Dania said quietly. "We built that whole volcano. You extracted the baking soda from the cupboard yourself because I was too short to reach."

Lucas almost smiled, then caught something odd in her voice. "Wait. Why do you sound like it already ended?"

She pulled a folded paper from her backpack. It was a withdrawal form, signed by a parent, dated that morning. "It's voluntary. I don't have to stay in debate. But you joined soccer without asking me, so I figured the study was right, and I should just stop pretending." She held the paper out like evidence at a trial. "I was going to hand it in at practice today."

The bus lurched around the corner by the rec center. Lucas looked at the form, then at the soccer field sliding past the window, then at her. "Don't hand it in on my account. Hand it in if you actually hate debate. Do you?"

"No," Dania admitted. "I love it. I just hated losing you."

"Then keep it, and keep me too." He took the form from her hands, folded it into a paper airplane, and launched it toward the front of the bus. "New rule. We test the study. Every Friday, this seat, one thing we both still care about."

Dania caught the airplane as it boomeranged off the window. "Fine. First topic, volcanoes."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: A receipt lists every item and the amount paid, so reading it before leaving the till catches a scanning mistake while it is easy to fix.
story:
Alyssa slid the five-dollar bill across the counter, and the coins came back warm from the register. "Check your receipt before you go," the cashier said, tapping the slip of paper. She said it the same way she said everything, quick and bored, but Alyssa stood still and read it anyway. The paper smelled faintly of the milk crates stacked behind the till. There, in small gray print, the milk appeared twice, and the amount paid was higher than the price of one carton. The scanner had charged her for two.

She counted her change in her palm. Too little left over, and now she knew why. Ms. Martínez had given her exactly enough for one carton and nothing more, so the mistake mattered. "It scanned the milk twice," Alyssa said, holding out the receipt and pointing at the doubled line. The cashier squinted, then hit a button, and the difference came back in coins that clattered into the tray. Alyssa picked them up one by one and counted again, lips moving, until the numbers matched what she had worked out in her head.

Emiliano was waiting by the door, bouncing on his heels. He had wanted to come inside, but Alyssa had said no, this was her solo errand, the one Ms. Martínez had assigned her for the class breakfast. "Did you get extra for the brittle star cookies?" he asked hopefully. He had been talking about those cookies all morning, the ones with the thin sugar shells that cracked like ice when you bit them. Alyssa looked at the coins left in her hand and counted them against the cookie price taped to the window. Not enough for cookies and bus fare never mind that, not enough for cookies at all.

"Maybe tomorrow," she said, and Emiliano's shoulders dropped, just a little. On the walk back she passed the science room window, where someone had left a glass vessel, a big measuring jug, drying upside down on a rack. She thought of the receipt folded in her pocket, every item and every amount printed in order, like the lines on that jug marking exactly how much it held. That afternoon she watched Emiliano dismantle his sandwich at lunch, piece by piece, saving the cookie-shaped crackers for last, and she slid two quarters across the table to him. "For after school," she said. "Bring me the receipt."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
story:
Violet sat at the kitchen table trying to open a jar of pickles with one hand, which was impossible, and thinking about the word the doctor had used yesterday. "The break missed the growth plate," he had told her mother, and her mother had looked relieved, but nobody had explained why.

Francesco arrived after school with Dawson, who was carrying a stack of comics. They had declared a truce over the argument about whose fault the treehouse fall had been, since Violet had been the one who hit the ground, arm bending the wrong way under her.

"Did you ask him what a growth plate is?" Francesco asked, poking the edge of her cast with one finger.

"Sort of. He said near the ends of long bones there's cartilage, and that's where bones lengthen while you're a kid." Violet flexed her good hand. "So my arm is still going to grow the same as the other one."

Dawson frowned. "How do you know the break missed it, though? It's inside the bone. You can't see it."

That was exactly the problem Violet had been chewing on all morning. The doctor had looked at an X-ray, but she hadn't seen the picture herself, and she hadn't thought to ask. Something hidden inside her arm was deciding whether her right arm would match her left one for the rest of her life, and she had just accepted "good news" without checking. It reminded her of the time she'd blamed Dawson's wobbly plank without ever climbing up to test it herself. She'd been wrong then, too, probably. She still hadn't eliminated that possibility, and the truce didn't cover it.

"Your mom put the X-ray disc in the drawer," Francesco said. "The one by the fridge."

Violet stood so fast the pickle jar rolled off the table and Dawson caught it. She dug through the drawer, past a toxic-looking bottle of old glue and a tangle of batteries, until her fingers found the paper sleeve. She slid the film out and held it up to the window light, a pale ghost of her own bones, the crack thin as a hair.

"Get me the ruler," she said. "We're measuring where the break ends."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: In many cities, each councillor is elected to represent one area of the city, often called a ward.
story:
The letter from the city lay open on Grandma's kitchen table, and Emma read it twice before she dared say anything out loud. The community garden behind the library would be paved over for a parking lot unless someone convinced a councillor to change the bylaw before the vote on Friday. Grandma grew her tomatoes there, and so did half the seniors on her street. "Grandma," Emma said slowly, "who's our councillor?" Grandma peered at the letter. "It doesn't say. It just says contact your local representative." That was the problem, and it itched at Emma all afternoon.

She remembered the spring, when the beehives at school had died off and no one knew why. Finlay had insisted it was vandals, but Emma had tracked the blooming bushes along the fence and realized the bees had simply lost their source of nectar when the groundskeeper cut everything down. Things fail for hidden reasons, she had learned, and you have to look for the cause underneath. Maybe politics worked the same way. If every councillor governed a different slice of the city, then emailing the wrong one would be like writing to a beekeeper about a bush two towns over.

She found the city website on Grandma's old laptop and clicked through maps, but the lines wiggled everywhere and the names meant nothing to her. Sophia texted back "just email the mayor" when Emma asked, which felt too easy. Emma sat very still, staring at the address bar, and then it struck her: she could type Grandma's street address into the ward finder. The cursor blinked. She pressed enter, and the screen hung there, white and blank, for what felt like a full minute.

Then the map bloomed with colour. A shape wrapped around Grandma's neighbourhood, labeled Ward 4. Emma turned to Grandma, hardly believing it. "This is a ward," she said. "In lots of cities, each councillor is elected to represent one area, and that area is called a ward." Grandma leaned in, squinting. "So there's one councillor just for us?" Emma nodded and copied the name and the email address onto a pad of paper.

They drafted the message together at the kitchen table. Emma wrote that the garden was fundamental to the street, that seniors depended on it, and that the bylaw should be changed to protect it. She kept it short and polite, the way Mr. Shapiro had taught them for persuasive writing back in September. Then she read it aloud, one last time, her finger under each line. Grandma reached over her shoulder and clicked Send.
